metadata.title: Gut Check Hype Meter claims dataset
metadata.author: Aaryav Sharma
metadata.description: Every popular gut-brain claim graded in the textbook Gut Check, with its evidence grade (Strong, Moderate, Preliminary, Hype), the reasoning, what would change the grade, and the sources linked in the card.

claims.chapter_title: The Brain in Your Belly (and Why That Phrase Is Misleading)
claims.claim: Your gut can move food without your brain
claims.verdict: Strong. Since 1755, scientists have watched isolated pieces of intestine, cut off from the brain and spinal cord, keep making propulsive movements, and modern experiments on animal intestine show the same thing. The small intestine keeps its between-meal contraction cycles after the vagus nerve is cut, and children with Hirschsprung disease show that losing the local neurons, not the brain connection, is what stops the bowel.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Very little. It rests on more than two centuries of consistent experiments plus human disease evidence.

claims.chapter_title: The Brain in Your Belly (and Why That Phrase Is Misleading)
claims.claim: Your gut is a second brain that thinks and feels
claims.verdict: Hype. The part about the gut having a large, independent nervous system is Strong. But the research describes the ENS running reflexes for movement, secretion, blood flow, and immune and barrier roles, not thinking, planning, or feeling. Gut sensations become feelings only when signals reach the brain.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Repeated, well-designed studies showing that enteric circuits by themselves do something more like choosing or learning than reflexes, in animals and then in people, could move the "thinks" part up to Preliminary.

claims.chapter_title: The Brain in Your Belly (and Why That Phrase Is Misleading)
claims.claim: Your gut has more neurons than your brain
claims.verdict: Hype. The ENS has about 400 to 600 million neurons by common estimates, roughly as many as the spinal cord. The brain has about 86 billion, well over a hundred times more, based on cell counts in adult human brains.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Nothing realistic. Even the highest gut estimates are far below the brain count.

claims.claim: 80% of your vagus nerve sends signals up to your brain
claims.verdict: Moderate. That most vagus fibers are sensory is well supported by anatomy reviews. The specific "80%" comes from old fiber counts in cats, and a careful 1990 rat study found that motor fibers in the abdominal vagus may be over a quarter of the total. The general claim ("most vagus fibers carry signals to the brain") would rate Strong; the exact percentage, applied to humans, is an approximation.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: A modern, careful fiber count of human vagus nerves, branch by branch, could confirm or revise the number.

claims.claim: Your gut cells are wired straight to your brain
claims.verdict: Preliminary. In mice, some gut sensor cells (neuropod cells) form synapses with vagal sensory neurons and pass signals within milliseconds, connecting the gut lining to the brainstem through one synapse plus the vagus nerve. These studies are careful, but they are mouse studies in a very new field, and "straight to your brain" skips the vagal neuron in between.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Finding the same synapses and fast signaling in human gut tissue, and then showing they matter for how people sense food, would move it to Moderate or higher.

claims.claim: Cold plunges, humming, or gargling reset your vagus nerve and cure anxiety
claims.verdict: Hype. Small lab studies in healthy adults show that brief cold on the face or neck, or slow breathing, can briefly shift heart rate and HRV, which are indirect estimates of vagal activity at the heart. None of the studies used in this chapter show that these tricks "reset" the vagus nerve, change gut function, or treat an anxiety disorder. "Reset" has no scientific meaning here.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Randomized controlled trials in people with anxiety, comparing a specific practice with a believable placebo practice over weeks, measuring anxiety symptoms (not just HRV), could move a specific technique, such as slow breathing, up to Preliminary or Moderate. Anxiety treatments that already have strong evidence are covered in Chapter 18.

claims.claim: C-section babies start life with different gut microbes
claims.verdict: Strong (for early differences). Large human studies, including a UK study of 596 newborns and the 903-child TEDDY study, confirm that birth mode changes which microbes colonize a baby in the first weeks and months. These differences shrink over the first year or so, and breastfeeding has a larger effect on maturation. Claims that C-section birth causes lifelong disease through the microbiome are a different matter: the studies in this chapter don't show that, so any long-term health claim is Preliminary at best.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Long-term studies that follow children for years and test whether early microbe differences actually cause later health differences, while accounting for the reasons a C-section was needed, would tell us whether the long-term claims hold up.

claims.claim: One round of antibiotics ruins your microbiome forever
claims.verdict: Hype (as stated). Human studies show that antibiotics quickly reduce gut diversity, and that recovery can be incomplete, with a few species missing for months in some people. But the same studies show that most of the community regrows within weeks to a couple of months in healthy adults. "Ruins forever" turns a real, modest, long-lasting change into a scare, and it can push people to avoid antibiotics they need.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: A careful version, "antibiotics can leave small, lasting changes in the gut microbiota," is well supported (Moderate to Strong). Long-term studies showing that those lasting changes harm health would strengthen the case for caution, which doctors already practice by prescribing antibiotics only when needed.

claims.claim: A home microbiome test can tell you what to eat to improve your mood
claims.verdict: Hype. The sequencing itself can be real science, but a 2024 international consensus statement by dozens of microbiome experts (Porcari and colleagues, Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology) concluded that evidence for using gut microbiome tests in clinical care is scarce, and that direct-to-consumer tests are sold without agreed regulation or any proven clinical value. No one has defined what a "healthy" microbiome looks like (Section 3.11), so there is no validated standard to compare your sample to, and no trials show that following a kit's advice improves mood.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Validated reference ranges for specific microbiome features, plus randomized trials showing that test-guided diet changes improve a specific health outcome compared with general advice, could move a specific test up.

claims.chapter_title: The Immune System as a Sense Organ
claims.claim: 70% of your immune system lives in your gut
claims.verdict: Hype. The most systematic count of human immune cells (Sender et al., 2023) found that the gut holds about 3% of all immune cells and about 5% of lymphocytes. What is true is that about 70% of antibody-making plasma cells are in the gut. The popular version turns a fact about one cell type into a claim about the whole system, often to sell a gut supplement.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: A new, careful whole-body count by a different method that found most immune cells in the gut. The 2023 count and the earlier 2007 review point the opposite way, so this is unlikely.

claims.chapter_title: The Immune System as a Sense Organ
claims.claim: Your gut bacteria control your brain's immune cells
claims.verdict: Preliminary. In mice, the complete absence of gut microbes left microglia immature, and microbial chemicals (short-chain fatty acids) helped them recover (Erny et al., 2015). Whether normal differences in human gut microbes change human microglia in a meaningful way has not been shown. "Control" overstates even the mouse results, which show influence, not command.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Human studies, for example brain imaging or tissue studies linking specific microbial chemicals to microglial activity, ideally followed by trials that change those chemicals and track brain immune markers.

claims.chapter_title: The Immune System as a Sense Organ
claims.claim: Inflammation causes depression
claims.verdict: Moderate. The link is real and repeated: people with depression have higher average inflammation markers (107 studies, more than 10,000 people), experimental inflammation lowers mood in healthy adults, and cytokine treatments can trigger depression. But not every depressed person is inflamed, an anti-TNF drug did not treat depression overall, and depression has many causes, including genes, stress, and life events. "Inflammation can contribute to depression in some people" is Moderate; "inflammation causes depression" as a blanket rule overstates it.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Large randomized trials showing that lowering inflammation reliably improves depression in people chosen for high inflammation would move it toward Strong. Repeated failures in such trials would move it down.

claims.chapter_title: Chemical Messengers and the Serotonin Myth
claims.claim: 90% of your serotonin is in your gut, so your gut controls your happiness
claims.verdict: Hype. The number is Strong: more than 90% of the body's serotonin is made in the gut, mostly by enterochromaffin cells. But that serotonin does not cross the blood-brain barrier, and the brain makes its own from tryptophan using a different enzyme (TPH2). Gut serotonin mainly runs gut movement, secretion, sensations like nausea, and platelet storage. The gut does send signals to the brain through nerves and other routes, but "gut serotonin controls your mood" is not what the evidence shows.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Human studies showing that changing gut serotonin production, by itself, reliably changes brain serotonin and mood. Drugs designed to lower gut serotonin without entering the brain would be a natural way to test this.

claims.chapter_title: Chemical Messengers and the Serotonin Myth
claims.claim: Depression is caused by low serotonin
claims.verdict: Hype. A 2022 umbrella review of 17 studies found no consistent evidence that depression is caused by lowered serotonin, and depression is widely understood to have more than one cause. Critics of that review argue that the serotonin system is disturbed in some people with depression (Jauhar 2023; Erritzoe 2023), and serotonin may be involved in how some treatments work. But even those critics describe a role for serotonin, not a single cause, so the simple cause-and-effect slogan is not supported. This grade is about the slogan only; it is not a judgment on whether antidepressants help, which is a separate question.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Consistent, repeated human evidence that serotonin activity is reduced before depression begins, and that restoring it reliably prevents or ends depression.

claims.chapter_title: Chemical Messengers and the Serotonin Myth
claims.claim: Gut bacteria make neurotransmitters that reach your brain
claims.verdict: Hype, as stated. The first half is real: it's well shown in lab cultures that common gut bacteria make GABA and other neurotransmitter molecules, and in mice that bacteria raise the gut's own serotonin production. But the "reach your brain" part is not shown in people: most of these molecules act in the gut, and human links between microbes and depression (about 1,000 people in one major study) are correlations.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Human studies tracing a microbe-made molecule from the gut into the brain, followed by controlled trials showing that changing those microbes changes brain chemistry and mood.

claims.chapter_title: Fiber, Fatty Acids, and the Blood-Brain Barrier
claims.claim: Butyrate helps protect the gut lining
claims.verdict: Moderate. In mice, butyrate is the main fuel for colonocytes (Donohoe 2011) and helps build calming regulatory T cells that protect against colitis (Smith 2013; Furusawa 2013). In people, the evidence is real but small: the colon lining takes up butyrate preferentially (Cummings 1987, autopsy data), colon cells from surgery specimens burn it as a main fuel (Roediger 1980, lab study), and in 4 patients with diversion colitis (inflammation in a stretch of colon cut off from the stool stream after surgery) rinsing that stretch with SCFAs cleared the inflammation over four to six weeks (Harig 1989). But a later double-blind trial in 13 patients found that two weeks of SCFA rinses worked no better than salt water (Guillemot 1991). What's missing is strong evidence from larger human trials that raising butyrate improves the gut lining or prevents disease.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Randomized trials in people showing that raising colon butyrate (through diet or another route) improves measured barrier function or disease outcomes would move this up. Trials showing no effect would move it down.

claims.chapter_title: Fiber, Fatty Acids, and the Blood-Brain Barrier
claims.claim: Leaky gut causes autism, depression, and everything else
claims.verdict: Hype. Intestinal permeability is real and can be measured, and it rises in some diseases and stressful states. But reviews describe the human data as mostly correlative, no disease has been cured by fixing permeability, and "leaky gut syndrome" is not a recognized diagnosis. Popular zonulin blood tests don't reliably measure zonulin.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Large human studies showing that increased permeability comes before a specific condition, plus randomized trials showing that repairing the barrier prevents or improves that condition, could move a narrow version of the claim (one condition, not "everything") toward Preliminary.

claims.chapter_title: Fiber, Fatty Acids, and the Blood-Brain Barrier
claims.claim: Short-chain fatty acids protect the human blood-brain barrier
claims.verdict: Preliminary. In germ-free mice, the BBB is leakier and microglia are immature, and adding microbes or butyrate partly reverses this (Braniste 2014; Erny 2015). But no human study has shown that gut microbes or SCFAs change BBB permeability. The one small human trial of colon-delivered SCFAs (66 men, one week) found a lower cortisol response to stress, not a change in the brain barrier or mood.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Human studies that measure BBB permeability directly (for example, with brain imaging) before and after changes in gut SCFAs, repeated in larger and more varied groups, would be needed to move it up. Animal research in general has a mixed record: only about one in three highly cited animal studies were later tested successfully in human trials.

claims.claim: Stress can physically change how your gut works
claims.verdict: Moderate. Small human experiments show that CRH speeds up the colon (10 people with IBS and 10 controls; Fukudo 1998) and that public-speaking stress raises small-intestine permeability in people whose cortisol rises (23 and 13 volunteers; Vanuytsel 2014). Mast cells near nerves are linked with pain in IBS (44 patients; Barbara 2004), and animal studies fill in the mechanisms. What's still unclear is how big these effects are in everyday life and how much they explain symptoms in each person.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Larger human studies that repeat these findings, especially ones that follow people through real-life stress like exam weeks and measure gut function directly, would move this toward Strong.

claims.claim: Stress causes IBD
claims.verdict: Hype. NIDDK lists immune, genetic, environmental, and microbial factors as possible causes of Crohn's disease, and stress isn't among them. The human evidence that does exist links stress to flares in people who already have IBD (704 people followed for a year; Bernstein 2010), which is a narrower and better-supported claim, worth about Moderate on its own. Blaming people for causing their IBD with stress is not supported and can be harmful.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: A few large studies have looked forward in time. In one, about 150,000 US women in the Nurses' Health Study who reported recent depressive symptoms were later diagnosed with Crohn's disease about 2.4 times as often (but not ulcerative colitis; Ananthakrishnan 2013). That's an association with low mood, not proof that stress causes IBD, and early, undiagnosed disease could explain part of it. If you have Crohn's disease and have felt down, this does not mean your feelings caused your illness. Repeated studies like this that measure stress itself, account for genes, smoking, and early symptoms, and find the same result in different groups would be needed to move "stress causes IBD" up to Preliminary.

claims.claim: Your gut bacteria control your stress response
claims.verdict: Preliminary. In mice, the evidence is strong: germ-free mice have exaggerated stress-hormone responses, and early colonization with microbes partly prevents this (Sudo 2004), while stress itself changes mouse gut microbes (Bailey 2011). In humans, the evidence is limited to small, short trials such as one week of colon-delivered SCFAs in 66 healthy men, which lowered the cortisol response to stress (Dalile 2020). "Control" overstates even the mouse findings.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Larger randomized trials in people of different ages and sexes, showing that a specific microbial change reliably changes the stress-hormone response and how people feel, would move this toward Moderate.

claims.claim: In IBS, the brain's pain brakes don't work
claims.verdict: Preliminary. In a 2004 human study of 20 women, a painful ice-water stimulus to the foot reduced rectal pain in healthy women but not in women with IBS, and a meta-analysis of brain scanning studies found differences in a region involved in pain control. These are small or correlational studies, and "don't work" overstates them: the brakes may work differently in some people, not fail in everyone.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Larger studies with men and women, repeated in different labs, that show weaker descending control predicts who develops IBS pain (not just who already has it), would move it toward Moderate.

claims.claim: People with IBS feel gut stretch as painful at lower levels, on average
claims.verdict: Strong. Human balloon studies since 1973 have repeatedly found that, as a group, people with IBS report pain at lower stretch than people without it (55% vs 6% at one volume in the first study), and a 2018 analysis of 1,144 patients in five cohorts linked higher sensitivity to worse symptoms. The words "on average" matter: many people with IBS have normal sensitivity on testing.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Little would lower the group finding. Studies showing exactly why some people become hypersensitive, and whether treating it improves symptoms for that subgroup, would add the missing "why."

claims.claim: If your tests are normal, the pain is in your head
claims.verdict: Hype. Standard tests look for structural disease, not for how sensitive the pain system is. Human balloon studies since 1973 show that many people with IBS feel normal gut stretch as painful while their gut wall tension is normal, and brain scans show real differences in how the brain processes gut signals. Pain always involves the brain, but that makes it real, not imaginary.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Nothing realistic. The careful version, "normal tests can mean the pain comes from a sensitized pain system rather than damage," is already well supported.

claims.chapter_title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Ulcerative Colitis and Crohn's
claims.claim: IBD is caused by stress
claims.verdict: Hype. No good evidence shows that stress causes IBD to start; the causes involve genes, the immune system, gut microbes, and the environment. One large study of more than 150,000 US nurses found that women with recent depression symptoms were more likely to be diagnosed with Crohn's disease later (but not ulcerative colitis), an association that doesn't show cause (Ananthakrishnan and colleagues, 2013). A 2009 review by Singh, Graff, and Bernstein found strong evidence for an association between perceived stress and flares in people who already have IBD, and a weaker link with stressful life events. That is correlation, not cause: a flare can raise stress just as easily as stress might nudge a flare.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: More large, long-term studies following healthy people before diagnosis, showing that stress consistently predicts who develops IBD after accounting for genes, smoking, and other factors, plus evidence of how it would work. Even then, "stress is one risk factor" would be very different from "stress causes IBD."

claims.chapter_title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Ulcerative Colitis and Crohn's
claims.claim: Diet alone can cure Crohn's disease
claims.verdict: Hype. No diet has been shown to cure Crohn's disease. The real finding is narrower: the 2026 ECCO-ESPGHAN guideline update prefers exclusive enteral nutrition (a supervised liquid-formula treatment), or a structured exclusion diet combined with partial formula, to induce remission in children with lower-risk Crohn's. Inducing remission is not curing, and a nutrition therapy planned and monitored by a care team is not a diet plan sold online.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Long-term randomized trials showing that a specific diet keeps people in lasting remission with a healed lining, without medicine, would make a narrower claim worth grading. "Cure" would require the disease to stay gone for good.

claims.chapter_title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Ulcerative Colitis and Crohn's
claims.claim: Vagus nerve stimulation can treat Crohn's disease
claims.verdict: Preliminary. Bonaz and colleagues had shown that vagus nerve stimulation improved colitis in rats. In a 2016 pilot study, they implanted stimulators in 7 people with active Crohn's disease and followed them for 6 months. Two were removed from the study at 3 months because they got worse; five reached remission. With only 7 people and no comparison group, the study shows the approach is feasible, not that it works. Implanted vagus nerve stimulators are FDA approved for some other conditions, but not for Crohn's disease.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Larger randomized trials comparing real stimulation with sham (fake) stimulation in people with Crohn's, measuring both symptoms and healing of the gut lining.

claims.chapter_title: IBS and Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction
claims.claim: Low-FODMAP should be a forever diet
claims.verdict: Hype. The low-FODMAP diet is designed as a short elimination phase followed by reintroduction, so that people end up avoiding only the foods that bother them. The trials that support it (13 trials, 944 patients in the 2022 meta-analysis) mostly tested short elimination periods, not lifelong restriction. Cutting out many foods for good can make eating stressful, make family meals and cultural foods harder, and limit the variety of foods (and fiber) that gut microbes use.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Long-term trials showing that permanent strict restriction works better and is safe compared with reintroduction and personalization. No such evidence exists.

claims.chapter_title: IBS and Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction
claims.claim: Gut-directed hypnotherapy helps IBS
claims.verdict: Moderate. In a 2020 network meta-analysis of 41 randomized trials (4,072 adults), gut-directed hypnotherapy was one of the therapies with the best evidence for improving IBS symptoms, along with CBT, and a 2024 analysis of 42 trials found it also helped belly pain. These are real human trials. But many had a high risk of bias, it's hard to "blind" people to whether they're getting hypnotherapy, and the authors said the benefits may be overestimated. The ACG suggests gut-directed psychotherapy for IBS.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Larger, well-designed trials with strong control conditions and long follow-up, including in teens, could move it up to Strong. Trials showing the benefit disappears against a good placebo-like control would move it down.

claims.chapter_title: IBS and Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction
claims.claim: IBS is just anxiety
claims.verdict: Hype. Anxiety and depression are more common in people with IBS: a 2019 meta-analysis of 73 studies (Zamani and colleagues) found anxiety symptoms in 39.1% and depression symptoms in 28.8%. A diagnosed anxiety disorder was present in about 23%, so most people with IBS don't have one. Stress can worsen gut symptoms (Chapter 7), but IBS also involves measurable changes in gut sensitivity and movement, and it can start after a gut infection. The 2020 Lancet review notes that it isn't clear whether psychological symptoms come before IBS or are driven by it. A brain-gut therapy helping IBS doesn't prove IBS is "psychological"; it shows the gut-brain link is two-way.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Nothing likely. The evidence points to a two-way gut-brain disorder, not to anxiety alone.

claims.claim: People with IBD have higher rates of anxiety and depression symptoms
claims.verdict: Strong (as an association). A 2021 meta-analysis of 77 studies and 30,118 adults found anxiety symptoms in about a third and depression symptoms in about a quarter of people with IBD, with higher rates during active disease, and IBS shows a similar pattern. That analysis measured how common the symptoms are rather than comparing people with IBD to people without it. Studies that did make the comparison point the same way: in a 2023 Danish registry study of 22,103 people with IBD and 110,515 matched people without it, those with IBD were more likely to have hospital-recorded anxiety and depression, both before and for at least ten years after diagnosis, and a 2024 UK study of 3,898 children and young adults (ages 5 to 25) with IBD found more new diagnoses of depression and anxiety than in matched peers. For IBS, the 2019 meta-analysis found about three times the odds of anxiety and depression symptoms compared with healthy people. These are questionnaire symptoms, not diagnoses, and they describe a link, not a cause.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Very little would weaken the association itself. Large studies in teens using the same questionnaires would sharpen the picture for younger readers. (See the Hype Meter for what each grade means.)

claims.claim: Gut bacteria from depressed people cause depression
claims.verdict: Preliminary. In 2016, two animal studies found that moving gut microbes from people with major depression into rats or germ-free mice led to depression-like behavior. Human studies show that people with depression have somewhat different gut bacteria, but these are snapshots that can't show direction. That microbes can change rodent behavior is reasonably supported; that they cause depression in people is not shown.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Long-term human cohort studies showing microbe changes come before depression, plus well-controlled human trials in which changing the microbes changes mood, would move it up.

claims.claim: Fixing your gut will fix your depression
claims.verdict: Hype. The gut-mood link is real and two-way, but the evidence that gut changes cause human depression comes mostly from rodent transfer studies and one-time snapshots. Depression has many causes, mood symptoms stay common even when IBD is inactive, and proven treatments (talk therapy, medication, or both) work on the brain directly. Promising that gut fixes will cure depression can lead people to delay care that works.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Large, long, well-controlled human trials showing that a specific gut treatment reliably relieves depression, compared with placebo, could support a narrower claim for some groups of people.

claims.claim: Celiac disease can affect your nerves and brain, not just your gut
claims.verdict: Moderate. Human studies consistently link celiac disease with peripheral neuropathy (reported in up to 39% of patients across small studies) and, less often, gluten ataxia (0% to 6%), and NIDDK lists nervous system symptoms as part of the disease. But the studies are small and varied, the exact mechanism is unclear, and the evidence that the gluten-free diet helps comes from observation, not randomized trials.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Large studies that follow people from diagnosis with careful nerve testing, plus a clear mechanism, could move it to Strong.

claims.claim: Gluten damages everyone's brain
claims.verdict: Hype. The best available test in people without celiac disease, a 2021 study of 13,494 US women, found no difference in memory and thinking scores between women who ate the most gluten and those who ate the least, over decades of diet records. The authors concluded their results do not support cutting gluten to protect thinking in people without celiac disease or established gluten sensitivity. Nervous system problems are a real concern for people with celiac disease, not proof of harm for everyone.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Repeated randomized trials showing that people without celiac disease think better after cutting gluten than after a disguised placebo diet. No such evidence exists.

claims.claim: Many people who think they're gluten sensitive are really reacting to fructans
claims.verdict: Preliminary. Blinded studies point away from gluten for many people: in one double-blind crossover trial of 59 adults, symptom scores were highest with fructan (clearly higher than with gluten), while gluten matched placebo, and an earlier trial of 37 adults found gluten-specific effects in only 8%. But these are small, short studies of adults, results differ between trials, and other wheat components may matter for some people.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Larger blinded trials in several countries, including teens, that test gluten, fructans, and other wheat parts separately and find the same pattern would raise it to Moderate.

claims.claim: Autistic children have more gut symptoms on average
claims.verdict: Strong (as an association). A 2014 meta-analysis of 15 comparison studies found that autistic children had higher odds of general GI symptoms (about 4.4 times), constipation, diarrhea, and belly pain. The link is consistent across studies, though the size varies and the causes are not known. This grade is about the association; it does not mean the gut causes autism.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Very little would undo the association. Large studies with standard symptom measures would pin down how big it is and why it happens.

claims.claim: Fecal transplants cure autism
claims.verdict: Hype. The best-known study treated just 18 autistic children with GI problems in an open-label trial with no placebo group; GI symptoms improved, but the design can't show cause. A 2024 placebo-controlled trial of 103 autistic children found no significant difference from placebo on its main behavior measure. And autism is a lifelong neurodevelopmental difference, not a disease to cure.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Nothing would make "cure" the right word. For the separate question of whether microbiome treatments can ease GI symptoms in autistic people, large placebo-controlled trials with gut symptoms as the main outcome would give a real answer; right now that question is Preliminary.

claims.claim: Gut bacteria cause autism
claims.verdict: Hype. One of the most carefully controlled human studies (247 children, 2021) found negligible direct links between autism and the microbiome once diet was considered, and a pooled analysis found autism-linked microbial patterns disappeared in sibling comparisons. The strongest causal evidence comes from mouse models, which can't capture what autism is. NIMH points to genes and early development, not gut bacteria.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Large studies that follow babies from birth, measure diet carefully, and show microbiome differences appearing before any signs of autism, replicated in several countries, would be needed to even reach Preliminary.

claims.claim: Parkinson's can start in the gut
claims.verdict: Moderate (as a hypothesis for some patients). Human autopsy studies show Lewy pathology early in the vagus nucleus and sometimes in gut nerves, large observational studies show constipation can come more than 10 years before diagnosis, and mouse experiments show misfolded alpha-synuclein can travel from gut to brain along the vagus nerve. But human evidence is mostly correlation, studies of vagus surgery and appendix removal in people disagree, and some patients don't fit the pattern at all. Saying "Parkinson's starts in the gut" for everyone is too strong; "Parkinson's may start in the gut in some people" is a fair summary, and that narrower claim is what this grade covers.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Long-term human studies that track alpha-synuclein in the gut and brain of the same people over many years, and show the gut changes come first and predict who develops the disease, could move it up. Large studies showing no gut-first group would move it down.

claims.claim: Removing your appendix prevents Parkinson's
claims.verdict: Hype. One large 2018 study linked appendix removal to lower Parkinson's risk, but a Danish study of 265,758 people found a slightly higher risk, and two meta-analyses (6 studies with about 3.55 million people, and 9 studies in 2025) found no overall link. No study tested appendix removal as prevention, and surgery has its own risks.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: New, large studies that consistently find lower risk after appendix removal, with a clear biological explanation, could move the association to Preliminary. Even then, it would not make surgery a prevention strategy.

claims.claim: Probiotics prevent Alzheimer's
claims.verdict: Hype. People with Alzheimer's have different gut bacteria in small studies, such as one comparing 25 patients with 25 matched controls, and mouse studies (summarized in a 2024 review by Seo and Holtzman) suggest microbes may affect amyloid buildup in mice. But a 2024 review describes the field as being in its infancy, and no large, long human trial has shown that any probiotic prevents Alzheimer's. The difference in microbes could be a result of the disease or of lifestyle, not a cause.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Large, long randomized trials in people, following them for years and showing fewer Alzheimer's diagnoses or slower decline with a specific product, could move it to Preliminary or higher. You'll learn how to read probiotic trials in Chapter 16.

claims.claim: Eating lots of ultra-processed food is linked to depression
claims.verdict: Moderate. (The stronger claim that ultra-processed food causes depression is not shown.) Large pooled analyses of observational studies (17 studies and 385,541 people in 2022; nearly 10 million people across a 2024 umbrella review) consistently link more ultra-processed food with more depression and anxiety symptoms. But most studies are snapshots, the evidence quality was rated low, money and stress can affect both diet and mood, and low mood can change what people eat. "Linked to" is accurate; "causes" is not shown.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Randomized trials that change ultra-processed food intake while keeping other things equal, and that measure mood over months, could upgrade the causal claim. Long prospective studies that carefully account for income, sleep, and earlier mood would also help.

claims.claim: Eating a Mediterranean diet treats depression
claims.verdict: Preliminary. A few small randomized trials, including SMILES (67 adults, 12 weeks, remission 32.3% vs 8.0%) and HELFIMED (152 adults, diet plus fish oil), found improvements when diet support was added to usual care. A meta-analysis of 16 trials found a small effect on depressive symptoms, and the large PREDIMED trial found no significant overall effect on new depression. The trials were small or short, participants knew their group, and diet was an add-on, not a replacement for therapy or medicine.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Several larger, longer trials, in different countries and age groups including teens, with careful comparison groups and consistent results, could move it to Moderate. A careful version of the claim: "Adding dietitian support may help some adults with depression, alongside usual treatment."

claims.claim: All probiotics are basically the same, so just grab any one
claims.verdict: Hype. A 2018 systematic review of 228 trials found that probiotic effects depend on both the specific strain and the specific condition, and NCCIH says a benefit from one strain doesn't carry over to others. Strains from the same species can behave differently, and a strain that helps one problem may not help another.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Large head-to-head trials showing that many different strains give the same benefit for the same condition. So far, the evidence points the other way.

claims.claim: Probiotics are always safe because they're natural
claims.verdict: Hype. Probiotics have a long record of apparently safe use in healthy people, but NCCIH says risk is greater for people with severe illness or weakened immune systems, and few studies have measured side effects in detail. In 2023, the FDA reported that probiotics given to hospitalized preterm infants contributed to invasive disease, including a death. "Natural" describes where something comes from, not how safe it is for a particular person.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Nothing about the "always" part. Better safety studies could show more precisely who is at risk and who isn't.

claims.claim: Probiotics treat depression and anxiety
claims.verdict: Preliminary. Several meta-analyses of human randomized trials report some benefit, but the estimates range from small to large, the trials disagree a lot, and the results depend on the strain, the people, and the questionnaire. A 2024 review of 12 trials (707 people) found improvement on one depression scale but not on three others, and one of the best-designed add-on trials so far (Section 16.10) was a small pilot. No probiotic is approved to treat depression or anxiety.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Large, preregistered, placebo-controlled trials of a specific strain in people with a diagnosed condition, with one primary outcome, that are then repeated by independent teams.

claims.claim: Poop transplants cure autism and Parkinson's
claims.verdict: Hype. For autism, the best-known study had 18 children, no placebo group, and participants who knew they were treated, so it can't show cause. For Parkinson's, three small placebo-controlled trials found a mild benefit in one and no meaningful motor benefit in two. No FMT product is approved for either condition, and "cure" isn't supported by any study.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Large, placebo-controlled, repeated trials showing clear, lasting benefits would move specific, carefully worded claims (such as "improves GI symptoms in some autistic children") toward Preliminary or Moderate. "Cure" would still not fit.

claims.claim: Vagus nerve stimulation is FDA approved for depression
claims.verdict: Strong, with fine print. FDA records show that in July 2005 the implanted VNS Therapy System was approved as an add-on, long-term treatment for adults with chronic or recurrent depression who haven't responded to 4 or more adequate antidepressant treatments. The approval fact is solid. How well VNS works for depression is less clear-cut than the approval itself, so the evidence for its benefit is better described as Moderate, and it is not a first-choice treatment.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: The approval fact won't change unless the FDA changes the label. A version of the claim that drops the fine print ("VNS treats depression," implying anyone, any device) would earn a lower grade.

claims.claim: This $300 vagus nerve gadget fixes anxiety
claims.verdict: Hype. Consumer wellness gadgets are not the medical devices tested in clinical trials, and no vagus stimulator is FDA approved to treat anxiety. A 2021 meta-analysis of 16 sham-controlled studies in healthy people found ear stimulation did not change a common heart-rate sign of vagus activity. The approved, authorized, and cleared vagus-related devices are for epilepsy, treatment-resistant depression, rheumatoid arthritis, headaches, and (for one prescription ear stimulator) IBS pain in teens.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Large, sham-controlled trials of that specific device in people with diagnosed anxiety disorders, showing clear benefit, followed by an FDA decision for that use.

claims.claim: This sleep hack resets your gut bacteria
claims.verdict: Hype. Gut microbes do have daily rhythms, shown in mice and people (Thaiss 2014), but the experiments linking a disrupted clock to harmful microbe changes were done in mice. No human trial has shown that a sleep trick, supplement, or gadget "resets" the microbiome in a way that improves gut or mental health.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Randomized trials in people that change sleep timing, then measure both microbes and real symptoms over months, could move a carefully worded version of this claim to Preliminary.

claims.claim: Exercise helps with depression and anxiety symptoms
claims.verdict: Strong. A 2023 umbrella review combined 97 reviews of more than 1,000 randomized trials with over 128,000 adults and found medium-sized improvements in depression and anxiety symptoms from physical activity programs. The benefit shows up again and again across populations, which is why the grade is Strong. But most of the reviews had serious quality problems, trial participants can't be blinded, and a 2023 analysis of 21 trials in children and teens found a smaller benefit than in adults, so the exact size of the effect, especially for teens, is less certain than the direction.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Very little would move it down; large, high-quality trials in teens would make the evidence even more direct for this book's readers. Exercise is a support, not a replacement for other treatment when someone has depression.

claims.claim: Exercise changes your microbiome in ways that improve your mood
claims.verdict: Hype. Exercise does change gut microbes in people, but in the key human study (32 adults, 6 weeks), the changes were small, depended on body weight, mostly disappeared after stopping, and mood was not measured. No human study has shown that these microbe changes are why exercise helps mood. The mood benefit itself is Strong; the microbiome explanation is a popular story that the evidence does not yet support.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Studies that measure microbes and mood together, first in animals and then in people over months, and test whether blocking the microbe change also blocks the mood benefit, could move a carefully worded version of the link to Preliminary.

claims.claim: CBT and gut-directed hypnotherapy help IBS symptoms
claims.verdict: Moderate (near the top of the range). A 2020 network meta-analysis of 41 trials with 4,072 people found that CBT and gut-directed hypnotherapy reduced the chance of ongoing IBS symptoms, and a large 2018 trial of 436 adults found lasting benefits from home-based CBT. The ACG's 2021 guideline suggests gut-directed psychotherapy (a conditional recommendation), and a 2025 pediatric guideline recommends hypnotherapy and CBT. The grade stops short of Strong because many trials had a high risk of bias and the true benefit is probably smaller than reported.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: More large trials with strong control conditions (for example, comparing therapy with an equally engaging education program) and long follow-up could move it to Strong. These therapies help many people; they don't cure IBS.

claims.claim: IBD only happens in Western countries
claims.verdict: Hype. A 2017 review of 147 studies found rising IBD incidence in newly industrialized countries in Asia, Africa, and South America, and a 2025 analysis of 522 studies across 82 regions showed IBD moving through epidemiologic stages worldwide. IBD was first common in early industrialized regions, but it isn't limited to them.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Nothing realistic; the global data are large and consistent. The careful version: "IBD became common first in Western countries and is now rising in many other parts of the world."

claims.claim: South Asian migrants in the UK have higher ulcerative colitis rates than their white neighbors
claims.verdict: Moderate. Studies in Leicestershire found ulcerative colitis about 2.45 times as common in South Asians as in Europeans in the 1970s and 1980s, and higher, more extensive ulcerative colitis has been reported in several countries. But the data are older and regional, Crohn's disease was actually less common in the same group, and a 2018 pooled analysis wasn't statistically significant.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Large, recent, population-wide studies in several countries, reporting Crohn's and ulcerative colitis separately for specific South Asian communities, could move it up or down.

claims.claim: Eating more ghee (or any single traditional food) will heal Crohn's disease
claims.verdict: Hype. Crohn's disease is an immune-driven inflammatory condition, and according to NIDDK, researchers have not found that specific foods cause or worsen Crohn's symptoms. No trial has shown that ghee, or any single food from any culture, heals Crohn's. The diet treatment with real evidence is different: a special liquid formula that doctors prescribe for some children with Crohn's (Chapter 9), planned and monitored by the care team. Food still matters for nutrition, growth, comfort, and family connection, and a care team or dietitian can help plan meals that work during flares and remission.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Even reaching Preliminary would take controlled studies in people with Crohn's showing that a specific food lowers inflammation on scopes and blood tests compared with a control diet. Moving higher would take large randomized trials.

claims.chapter_title: Be Your Own Scientist: Reading Health Claims
claims.claim: This probiotic is proven to lower stress (it worked in a study!)
claims.verdict: Hype. The best-known "stress probiotic" study, Bravo 2011, was done in mice. When the same strain was tested in 29 healthy men for 8 weeks with a placebo comparison (Kelly 2017), it had no measurable effect on stress, mood, or thinking. Probiotic effects also depend on the exact strain, so a result for one strain doesn't transfer to others.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Several large, placebo-controlled trials of a specific strain in people with stress or anxiety problems, by independent teams, showing a consistent benefit. That could move the claim for that strain to Preliminary or Moderate.

claims.chapter_title: Be Your Own Scientist: Reading Health Claims
claims.claim: An FDA-approved microbiome pill helps stop C. diff from coming back
claims.verdict: Strong. A phase 3 (large, late-stage; see Chapter 17), double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 182 adults found recurrence of 12% with the treatment versus 40% with placebo at 8 weeks, and the FDA approved it as Vowst in 2023. The approval covers one specific use: preventing recurrence in adults 18 and older after antibiotic treatment for recurrent C. diff.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Longer follow-up showing safety problems, or failed replication. Note that the Strong grade does not extend to other uses, such as anxiety, autism, or weight; those would need their own trials.

claims.chapter_title: Be Your Own Scientist: Reading Health Claims
claims.claim: A new study found that...
claims.verdict: Preliminary, until you check. A single new study can be anything from a mouse experiment to a large trial, so the honest starting grade is "it depends." Most first-time findings, especially in mice or small groups, are Preliminary, and NCCIH reminds readers that one study rarely proves anything. A large, preregistered, randomized trial in people can earn more, especially when it agrees with earlier work.
claims.what_would_change_the_grade: Tracing the headline to the study. Human, randomized, large, preregistered, and replicated moves it up. Mouse-only, tiny, unregistered, or company-funded with no independent check keeps it at Preliminary or pushes it toward Hype if the headline overstates it.
